explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The verse says Joshua gave Caleb his portion "According to the LORD’s command to him…" So Joshua isn't making this up as he goes. He's handing out the land the way he was told, kind of like me following a recipe card instead of guessing at the flour (Joshua 15:13).

Nope, no ballots in this verse, friend. No clipboards, no show of hands. The text says Joshua gave Caleb his portion "According to the LORD’s command to him…" The command is what Joshua goes by (Joshua 15:13).

I get why you'd think so, since Hebron lands among the sons of Judah. But the verse never mentions a deal or any bargaining. It says Joshua gave Caleb a portion "According to the LORD’s command to him…" That command is the whole answer (Joshua 15:13).

You got it, baker. The verse says Caleb "…drove out from there the three sons of Anak…" the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. Three names, and Caleb drove them out of Hebron. I can't even clear my counter of crumbs without a fight (Joshua 15:14).

Hmm, not this time, friend. The verse never mentions tribute or any payment. The text says Caleb "…drove out from there the three sons of Anak…" What he does about them is drive them out (Joshua 15:14).

Not this one, baker. The text never mentions a treaty. It says Caleb "…drove out from there the three sons of Anak…" Those were the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. Driving them out is what he does (Joshua 15:14).

Right on, friend. Caleb says, "To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage." That's a big promise to put on the table. I think a man who says that out loud means to keep it (Joshua 15:16).
Not a servant, friend. Caleb names someone in his own family. He says, "…I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage." The one he promises is his daughter, and her name is Acsah (Joshua 15:16).

Not a sister, baker. Caleb talks about his own child. He says, "…I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage." That's what he promises to the man who captures Kiriath-sepher. Good thinking on the family angle, though (Joshua 15:16).
Not quite, friend. Caleb doesn't back out at all. After Othniel captures the city, the verse says "…Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage." A promise made, a promise kept (Joshua 15:17).

Yes, it's false, baker. The text says Othniel captured the city, and then "…Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage." Caleb doesn't back out. I think a promise kept like that must have felt good to see. Caleb did just what he said he would (Joshua 15:17).

That's it, friend. When Acsah gets off her donkey, Caleb asks her, "What do you desire?" Short and kind, and it opens the door for her to ask. I'd say that's a dad who wants to hear her out (Joshua 15:18).

Good thinking, since Othniel is part of the story. But the verse has Caleb asking something else. When she gets off her donkey, he says, "What do you desire?" His question is about what she wants (Joshua 15:18).
Nobody's checking the clock here, baker. Caleb doesn't ask how long she will stay. When she gets off her donkey, he asks, "What do you desire?" His question is about what she wants (Joshua 15:18).

True, baker! Acsah asks for springs, and the verse says "…Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs." She asked her dad for water, and he gave her both sets. I love that for her. Every dry spot in the Negev needs a spring or two (Joshua 15:19).
Oh, this one's a yes, friend. Caleb doesn't turn her down or hand over just half. The text says, "So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs." Both of them, upper and lower (Joshua 15:19).

Correct, baker. The text says "…the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." It's a little hard to read after that long list of cities, but the writer tells it straight. That's the one spot where Judah couldn't drive them out, and the verse says so plainly (Joshua 15:63).

That would be a tidy ending, friend, but it's not in the text. The verse never mentions peace or the Jebusites leaving. It says Judah "…could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." The Jebusites stay (Joshua 15:63).

Nope, it goes the other way. The text says the descendants of Judah "…could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." So the Jebusites are still there. Judah didn't finish that job (Joshua 15:63).

True, baker. The verse says, "So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah." So when this was written, they were still in Jerusalem. The writer ends the whole list on that note. It's plain and honest, and it sticks with you (Joshua 15:63).

Not false, friend. The text says, "So to this day the Jebusites live there among the descendants of Judah." At the time this was written, they were still living in Jerusalem. The story doesn't pretend otherwise (Joshua 15:63).
